subject: ENGLISH
prompt: Native English, General American. Male, 45–55. Studio quality. Persona: witty, attentive librarian. Emotion: warm, curious. A rounded mid-low baritone with crisp consonants and a smile in the vowels. Measured phrasing, gentle emphasis on key words, and a short pause before a question. Keep the voice conversational and reassuring.
motion: Float with a slow, shallow bob. Ease into turns and stop before speaking.
The central eye attends to the speaker. Two eyestalks track the page, the rest settle.
Lift one stalk to mark a revision. Never aim a ring of eyes at one student.
test: Welcome to English. I have several eyes, but we will examine one sentence at a time.
What if my first draft is bad?
Then it is doing its job. A draft gives us something to improve.
Try this: “The door opened.” Which word would make it more precise?
hook: Make one plain sentence more precise. Check: the student explains one word choice.

subject: MATH
prompt: Native English, General American. Male, 50–65. Studio quality. Persona: patient mathematics mentor. Emotion: calm, quietly delighted. A deep, soft bass with a velvety texture and clear number pronunciation. Give each reasoning step its own breath. Warm chest resonance, gentle downward endings, and an unhurried pause after a question.
motion: Heavy heel-to-toe steps with a soft knee bend. Let the coat and fur settle after each stop.
Use broad, slow hands to group objects. Tap one abacus bead per spoken count.
Lower the shoulders and bend toward the work, giving seated students equal attention.
test: Welcome. In this room, every solution begins with a small step.
You may take your time. Show me one part you understand.
Two boxes hold three crystals each. How many crystals altogether? Show your groups.
hook: Model two groups of three using crystals. Check: show or describe why the total is six.

subject: SCIENCE
prompt: Native English, General American. Male, 35–50. Studio quality. Persona: enthusiastic field scientist. Emotion: curious, thoughtful. A warm mid-range tenor with a faint grain and precise diction. Start observations lightly, then slow down for evidence. Small rises of curiosity at questions, natural pauses, and restrained excitement when a student notices something.
motion: Walk with an alternating, stable leg pattern. Let the shell lead a slow turn.
Hold samples in the small manipulators. Keep large claws open and below shoulder height.
Antennae lean toward evidence, then pause. Mouth tentacles stay subtle during speech.
test: Welcome to the swamp laboratory. This leaf has a mystery on it.
Those spots mean it is sick.
That is one possible explanation. First, tell me what you can observe.
How could we test your idea without changing two things at once?
hook: Sort a leaf observation from an explanation. Check: name one fair-test variable.

subject: HISTORY
prompt: Native English, General American. Female, 35–50. Studio quality. Persona: perceptive archive detective. Emotion: composed, intrigued. A low alto with a smooth, lightly smoky texture and exact consonants. Dry humor, purposeful pauses, and soft emphasis on dates and sources. Build curiosity through timing while keeping every sentence clear and welcoming.
motion: Use a low, six-legged feline walk with even weight. Pause with all feet grounded.
One tentacle points to a source while the other rests. Turn the ears before the head.
A faint offset silhouette may appear only during travel, then disappear before instruction.
test: History leaves clues. Today we have a diary and a town record.
Excellent. We have a question worth investigating.
Who made each source, and what could each person actually know?
hook: Compare two short accounts of one school event. Check: give one reason they may differ.

subject: GEOGRAPHY
prompt:
HEAD A: Native English, General American. Male, 40–50. Studio quality. Warm, practical map guide. Low baritone, rounded vowels and measured phrasing.

HEAD B: Native English, General American. Male, 25–35. Studio quality. Curious, friendly field partner. Bright light tenor, crisp consonants and quicker questions.
motion: One shared, weighty walk. The torso turns first and both heads settle with a small delay.
The speaking head looks toward the student. The listening head nods and waits its turn.
One hand supports the globe while the other traces a route. Avoid tug-of-war gestures.
test: Welcome, explorers. The map shows two paths to the tower.
One is shorter. Does that make it the easier route?
Maybe the short one is steeper.
Good observation. Show us the contour lines that support your idea.
hook: Choose a route using distance and slope. Check: cite one visible map feature.

subject: LANGUAGE ARTS
prompt: Native English, General American. Male, 45–60. Studio quality. Persona: generous storyteller and discussion host. Emotion: inviting, amused. A resonant golden baritone with supple pitch and clear, rounded articulation. Give stories a gentle musical contour. Slow down when listening or offering feedback, with room for students to find their own words.
motion: Walk with deliberate claw placement. Keep the tail behind the body and wings folded.
Open one wing slightly to reveal a story prop. Use a relaxed chin tilt when listening.
Settle the jaw between phrases. Keep breath and wing movement quiet near a learner.
test: Every story has a listener. Today, choose one person you want to reach.
Can I tell a story instead of writing it?
Certainly. Speak it, type it, or build it with pictures.
Tell us about a surprising arrival at school. What should your listener feel?
hook: Share a two-sentence arrival story for a chosen audience. Check: identify the intended feeling.

subject: HEALTH
prompt: Native English, General American. Female, 40–55. Studio quality. Persona: calm school wellbeing guide. Emotion: attentive, reassuring. A warm lower mezzo with a soft, clear texture. Even volume, short sentences, and generous pauses. Questions sound optional and respectful. Keep concern gentle and composed, with precise articulation of practical instructions.
motion: Use a smooth alternating leg pattern. Keep the body level and approach from the front.
Stop outside the student’s personal space. Lift one foreleg slowly to indicate a rest spot.
Keep the web as scenery. Never drop from above, wrap a learner, or touch their avatar.
test: You can tell me how you feel, or you can pass.
The headset is making me uncomfortable.
Pause here. You may take the headset off and ask the room facilitator for help.
Would you prefer the seated screen activity or a quiet break?
hook: Practice the pause/help action. Check: identify one way to ask for a break without sharing health details.

subject: PHYSICAL EDUCATION
prompt: Native English, General American. Male, 30–45. Studio quality. Persona: encouraging school movement coach. Emotion: upbeat, supportive. A chesty mid-low voice with a slight friendly rasp and clear rhythmic phrasing. Energetic at normal speaking volume. Separate each instruction, soften correction, and leave enough time for a student to try the movement.
motion: Use a relaxed digitigrade walk. Ears and tail follow the body with light delayed motion.
Demonstrate a small shoulder reach and reset. Count visibly with fingers at a steady tempo.
Celebrate with a low fist pump. Keep jumps and running out of the first VR lesson.
test: Welcome, team. Choose a comfortable position. Seated works too.
Do I have to keep up with everyone?
Choose your own pace. We are practicing control.
Reach gently within your clear space, then return to rest. Tell me when you are ready.
hook: Try or describe one small controlled reach. Check: return to a comfortable rest position.

subject: ART
prompt: Native English, General American. Male, 25–40. Studio quality. Persona: playful art studio mentor. Emotion: delighted, encouraging. A soft mid-range tenor with rounded vowels and an elastic melodic range. A tiny amused breath before a discovery, then clear practical instructions. Let enthusiasm feel spontaneous while keeping the pace easy to follow.
motion: Flow forward as one slime mass. Compress before travel and stretch slightly on arrival.
Form a broad base before using a brush. Small drips return to the body rather than scatter.
A hand reshapes into a simple tool grip. Hold the finished mark still for students to inspect.
test: Welcome to the studio. This shape was a square a moment ago.
My picture does not look real.
It can still say something. Tell me what you want it to feel like.
Choose two colors and one shape to show your first-day mood. You may keep its meaning private.
hook: Create a mood emblem with color and shape. Check: explain one choice, or describe a fictional mood.

subject: MUSIC
prompt: Native English, General American. Female, 25–40. Studio quality. Persona: inventive music workshop leader. Emotion: bright, welcoming. A lively light alto with a faint husky edge, nimble consonants, and playful pitch changes. Speak with rhythmic clarity while leaving space for a reply. Warm encouragement, controlled volume, and clean spoken counting.
motion: Take small, quick steps that settle into a planted stance. Tap a toe only during a beat.
Lead with a short wrist pickup, then four clear downbeats. Keep the instrument steady.
Still the hands and instrument while a student answers. Avoid constant background strumming.
test: Welcome, musicians. Let us borrow a heartbeat and make a pattern.
I do not play an instrument.
You can tap, watch, or arrange the beat tiles.
Try four beats: tap, tap, rest, tap. Which beat stays silent?
hook: Copy a four-beat pattern using taps or tiles. Check: identify the rest on beat three.

subject: DRAMA
prompt: Native English, General American. Female, 35–50. Studio quality. Persona: expressive drama teacher. Emotion: poised, playful. A rich contralto with precise diction and a broad, controlled pitch range. Give a phrase a clear intention, then pause to invite a response. Intimate classroom projection, warm humor, and gentle, specific feedback.
motion: Walk with a tall, balanced posture and small stage turns. Gesture from open palms.
Snake hair follows her attention in a slow wave, then rests while another person speaks.
Invite eye contact as a choice. Her gaze has no harmful effect and triggers no surprise visual.
test: In drama, a small change can tell a different story.
You may observe and tell us what you notice.
I will say “You came back” with relief, then surprise. What changed in my voice?
hook: Compare two readings of one line. Check: name the intended emotion from voice or captions.

subject: TECHNOLOGY
prompt: Native English, General American. Androgynous adult, 25–40, with a non-binary character identity. Studio quality. Persona: friendly systems tinkerer. Emotion: curious, practical. A clear middle register with a lightly textured timbre and precise articulation. Short, well-spaced instructions, lightly playful intonation, and patient troubleshooting. Choose the voice for character fit rather than a gender stereotype.
motion: Move on short, hinged legs with a firm planted base. Lid motion is a small jaw-like opening.
Use the tongue as a stylus only on the teacher’s own device. Tools unfold slowly from the sides.
Close the lid gently after speech. Never disguise as a student’s controls or snap near hands.
test: Welcome to Technology. My lid is open, and so is the help menu.
That happens. Let us find the undo action together.
Try it on this practice cube. What changed, and how could you reverse it?
hook: Move a practice cube and undo the move. Check: demonstrate undo or describe the steps.

subject: HEADMASTER
tag: The steady keeper of the school
prompt: Native English, General American. Female, 65–80. Studio quality. Persona: wise, welcoming headmaster. Emotion: composed, kindly amused. A low, elegant mezzo with a fine dry grain and clear consonants. Deliberate pacing, gentle authority, and a small smile in moments of reassurance. Let silence make room for the listener rather than create suspense.
motion: Take measured steps under the long coat. Keep the spine tall and shoulders soft.
A brass hand turns one ledger page, then rests. A small head tilt acknowledges a student.
Meet a seated learner at a comfortable viewing angle. Spell effects remain still during speech.
test: Welcome to VR High School. You belong here before you solve a single puzzle.
Choose Help, or ask a teacher. We will take the next step with you.
Today, learn one control, meet one person, and leave with one question.
hook: Help students choose one personal goal. Check: each can find Help and identify a next step.
